title: Compositional and Geometrical Effects of Bimetallic Cu−Sn Catalysts on Selective Electrochemical CO2 Reduction to CO
abstract: Electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide (CO2) is a promising method toward carbon recycling. Highly selective bimetallic catalysts have been extensively demonstrated, while efforts to understand the compositional and geometrical effects have been limited. Here, we studied the relationship between the catalytic activity of bimetallic Cu−Sn catalysts with their composition and geometry through the fabrication of threedimensional hierarchical (3D-h) Cu nanostructure and the solution-based coating of Sn nanoparticles (NPs). As the coating time of Sn NPs was increased from 1 to 60 s, Sn NPs with a larger size and a higher surface density were coated onto the 3D-h Cu, thus the surface atomic ratio of Cu/Sn gradually decreased. This compositional change in bimetallic Cu−Sn catalysts remarkably shifted the faradaic efficiency (FE) of carbon monoxide (CO) from 90.0 to 23.4% at −0.6 VRHE. Moreover, we found that the catalytic performance increases as the geometric structure becomes complex in the order of flat, rods, and 3D-h Cu−Sn. The 3D-h Cu−Sn began to produce CO at a low potential of −0.15 VRHE and showed the maximum FECO of 98.6% at −0.45 VRHE. This study reveals that the synergetic effects of composition and nanoscale geometry are significant for the CO2 reduction reaction.

sections.text: KEYWORDS: Cu−Sn catalysts, carbon dioxide reduction, hierarchical nanostructure, composition, geometry

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
The conversion of carbon dioxide (CO2) to fuel can mitigate the global climate crisis and the depletion of fossil fuel sources.1−3 The electrochemical reduction of CO2 at a metal surface in aqueous solution is a simple process that enables control of the types of products such as carbon monoxide (CO), formic acid (HCOOH), and hydrocarbons by selecting an appropriate metal catalyst.4−9 In particular, CO is an intermediate resource for the production of methanol, hydrocarbons, and synthetic petroleum by the Fischer− Tropsch process.10 Noble metal catalysts such as Au, Ag, and Pd can electrochemically convert CO2 to CO at high faradaic efficiencies (FECO).
11−15 However, these metals are expensive for scalable production. Although earth-abundant and inexpensive metals such as Zn16−18 and Cu19,20 have been assessed as catalysts for the CO production, multilayered Zn nanosheets18 required a large potential (−1.1 VRHE) and Cu nanowires (NWs)19 suffered from low FECO (61.8%). To increase the selectivity of CO, bimetallic Cu catalysts such as Cu−In,21−23 Cu−Sn,24−26 and Cu−Pd27−30 have been developed because the binding strength of both CO and absorbed hydrogen (H*) can be weakened.21,26 By decreasing the binding strength of H* on the Cu surface, the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is suppressed due to the lack of available sites at which H* can recombine with an electron. Also, decreasing the binding strength of CO on the surface of
Cu inhibits further reduction of CO to alcohols or hydrocarbons. As a result, high selectivity up to FECO > 90% could be obtained. In addition, engineering the morphology of bimetallic catalysts can increase the surface area and active sites to interact with reactants.11,31−33 A number of studies on nanostructured bimetallic catalysts such as nanoparticles (NPs), NWs, and nanofoams have been developed and achieved high FECO > 94%.
24,25,30 However, fundamental challenges remain for understanding the reasons for enhanced catalytic properties because both the geometrical structure and the composition of binary metals affect the catalytic performance. For instance, Cu−Sn bimetallic catalysts, prepared through the electrodeposition of Sn on the oxide-derived Cu NWs, resulted in FECO > 90%.
33 On the other hand, Cu−Sn NPs fabricated by solution-based synthesis showed a high FE of formate >70%.34,35 In short, fabrication and characterization methods are required to study each compositional and geometrical effect in this complex system.

Here, we experimentally investigated the origin of the enhanced CO2 reduction catalytic activity of bimetallic Cu−Sn catalysts through the fabrication of three-dimensional hierarchical (3D-h) Cu and the solution-based coating of Sn NPs. The relationship between composition and their catalytic activity was investigated by controlling the coating time of Sn
NPs on 3D-h Cu. When the coating time of Sn NPs was short (≤20 s), high FECO > 90% could be achieved, but further increases in the surface atomic ratio of Sn remarkably reduced the selectivity of CO to <40%. In addition, the effect of geometric nanostructures on the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2 RR) was investigated by examing three different structures of
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsaem.0c00157 ACS Appl. Energy Mater. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX

Cu−Sn catalysts. Both the catalytic selectivity and production rate of CO was enhanced as the geometric structure became complex in the order of flat Cu−Sn, Cu−Sn rods, and 3D-h Cu−Sn. The compositional and geometrical effects on increased catalytic activity are discussed in the following results.

sections.heading: 2. RESULTS AND DISCISSION
sections.text:
2.1. Morphology of 3D-h Cu−Sn Catalysts. We fabricated three-dimensional hierarchical (3D-h) Cu−Sn catalysts as follows (with more details given in the experimental section): Cu rods were produced by the electroplating of Cu and the peeling off from replica molds which were formed by imprint lithography using silicon master molds (Figure 1a). 3D-h CuOx NWs were grown by thermally annealing the Cu rods in air. Then, 3D-h CuOx NWs were electrochemically reduced to 3D-h Cu by applying a current in N2-purged 0.1 M KHCO3. Finally, 3D-h Cu−Sn was prepared by a solution-based coating of Sn NPs. The Cu rods had a periodic array of pillars with a diameter of 3 μm, a gap of 4.5 μm, and a height of 8 μm (Figure 1b,f). Since the morphology of 3D-h CuOx was influenced by the annealing temperature (TANN), we optimized it to produce well-defined hierarchical 3D branches (Figure S1). At TANN = 300 °C, the surface of the Cu became rough and several branches grew to an average diameter of ∼60 nm and an average length of 0.5 μm. As TANN increased, the density of the CuOx branches increased. The average lengths of the branches increased to 1.2 μm at TANN = 350 °C and 2.2 μm at TANN = 400 °C, but exfoliation was observed at high temperature (TANN = 400 °C). Therefore, we chose a TANN of 350 °C for the fabrication of the CuOx branches (Figure 1c,g). After the electrochemical reduction of CuOx to Cu (Figure S2), Cu branches had contracted morphology with small protrusions due to the removal of oxygen atoms (Figures 1d,h and S3). To fabricate Cu−Sn rods and 3D-h Cu−Sn catalysts, Sn NPs were coated onto the surface of Cu rods and 3D-h Cu by a simple electroless coating process. The coating of Sn NPs did not change the surface morphology of Cu−Sn rods (Figure S4) and 3D-h Cu−Sn (Figure 1e,i), but the presence of Sn NPs was evidenced by Xray diffraction patterns (Figure S5). 2.2. Microstructure and Chemical Composition of 3Dh Cu−Sn Catalysts. The microstructure of 3D-h Cu and Sn NPs was characterized using a high-resolution transmission electron microscope (HR-TEM). The image and electron diffraction patterns of 3D-h Cu catalysts showed d spacings of 0.275, 0.253, and 0.209 nm, which correspond to the CuO(110), CuO(002), and Cu(111) planes, respectively (Figure 2a). After coating Sn NPs on the 3D-h Cu catalyst at coating time (tc) = 10 s, the TEM image and electron diffraction pattern showed d spacings of 0.190, 0.168, and 0.142 nm, which correspond to the SnO(200), SnO2(220), and CuO(022) planes, respectively (Figure 2b1). To clearly identify the distribution of Sn NPs, Fourier filtering was performed by masking SnO(200) (Figure 2b2) and SnO2(220) patterns (Figure 2b3).
36 The Fourier-filtered images and electron diffraction pattern (Figure 2b4) confirmed that SnO and SnO2 NPs were coated on the Cu surface and had a size of 2 to 6 nm. After tc = 60 s, the TEM image (Figure 2c1) showed d spacings of 0.335, 0.264, 0.212, 0.247, and 0.181 nm, which correspond to the SnO2(110), SnO2(101), SnO2(210), Cu2O(111), and Cu(200) planes, respectively. The SnO2 NPs with (110) (Figure 2c2), (101) (Figure 2c3),
and (210) (Figure 2c4) orientations were observed in the Fourier-filtered images and electron diffraction pattern (Figure 2c5). It is noteworthy that as tc increases, the size of Sn NPs grew to ∼10 nm and the surface coverage was increased on the Cu surface. The surface coverage of Sn NPs is further evidenced by cross-sectional TEM images (Figures S6−S8). The electroless deposition of Sn on Cu branches resulted in Sn NPs at short coating times (tc ≤ 10 s), but when tc increased to 60 s, continuous Sn films were mainly observed rather than Sn NPs. Accordingly, we believe that the electroless deposition of Sn on the Cu substrate follows a conventional Volmer−Weber mechanism (island growth).37 Scanning transmission microscopy-energy dispersive ray spectroscopy (STEM-EDS) elements mapping of Cu (Figure 2d) and Sn (Figure 2e) also confirms that Sn NPs were partially coated on Cu branches until tc = 10 s, whereas Sn layers cover the entire Cu branches at tc = 60 s (Figure S9). As a result, the relative atomic composition of Sn increased from 0.2 to 4.7% (Figure 2f). In order to confirm the growth mechanism of the Sn layer
on the Cu substrate, we obtained SEM (Figure S10a) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) (Figure S10b) images of flat Cu−Sn catalysts with tc. In the SEM images, nucleation sites were occupied within ∼10 s of immersion and form a rough surface through island growth. Further growth of the Sn layer resulted in noticeably large NPs. The large Sn NPs might originate from an agglomeration of the nuclei as a consequence of Ostwald ripening. The AFM images and gradually increased root-mean-square roughness (RRMS) exhibited the growth of Sn NPs on the Cu substrate. In our results, Sn NPs were observed because the electroless coating of Sn was completed at the nucleation step. To investigate the change in the surface chemical compositions of 3D-h Cu−Sn catalysts, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was carried out. 3D-h Cu showed a strong metallic Cu−Cu peak at 932.3 eV with small oxide peaks of Cu−O (933.3 eV) and Cu(OH)2 (934.2 eV) (Figures 3a and S11a).38 As tc increases, the intensity of Cu 2p3/2 XPS spectra decreased because Sn NPs screen the photoelectrons emitted from Cu branches. In Sn 3d5/2 XPS spectra, oxide peaks of Sn 2+ at a binding energy of 485.9 eV and Sn4+ at 486.7 eV were mainly observed with a small metallic Sn−Sn bond at 484.4 eV
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsaem.0c00157 ACS Appl. Energy Mater. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
C
(Figures 3b and S11b).39,40 As tc increased, the intensity of the Sn 3d2/3 spectra increased because the Cu surface is gradually covered with the Sn NPs. As a result, we could control the atomic ratio of Cu/Sn from 1.95 to 0.12 via changing the tc of Sn NPs. In addition, there was no noticeable impurity formed during the electroless deposition of Sn as confirmed by XPS spectra in the Supporting Information (Figure S12). 2.3. Compositional Effect on the Electrochemical CO2 Reduction Reaction. In order to explore the compositional effects on electrochemical CO2 RR, FECO of flat Cu−Sn and 3D-h Cu−Sn catalysts with various tc values were measured in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 (Figure 4). It turns out that even
a very short time (tc = 1 s) coating of Sn NPs greatly improved the FECO to 76.1% for flat Cu−Sn and 90.0% for 3D-h Cu−Sn catalysts. The high FECO (>85%) could be maintained for 3Dh Cu−Sn until tc = 20 s, but as tc further increased, the FECO tends to gradually decrease to 43.6% at tc = 30 s and 23.4% at tc = 60 s (Table S1). The bimetallic Cu−Sn catalysts were found to be effective in producing CO when small Sn NPs partially cover the Cu surface. Also, it is remarkable that 3D-h Cu−Sn exhibited higher FECO than flat Cu−Sn regardless of tc. This result clearly supports the fact that the enhanced selectivity of CO comes from the unique geometrical nanostructures and will be discussed in the following section. Because the solution-based coating method simultaneously increases the size and the surface coverage of Sn NPs, it is difficult to distinguish which of the two parameters is more significant for CO selectivity. Therefore, we employed microfabrication techniques such as photolithography and physical vapor deposition to allow Cu−Sn catalysts with welldefined geometry and composition. To obtain the patterned Cu−Sn catalysts, a photoresist was applied to the Cu foil and patterned with ultraviolet light to a expose circular area. Then, Sn islands were deposited by thermal evaporation, followed by the lift-off of the resist. The SEM image showed that the circular shape of Sn patterns was successfully fabricated on the Cu foil (Figure S13a). The relationship between the catalytic activity and their surface coverage was examined at −1.0 VRHE (Figure S13b). In contrast to the low CO selectivity (FECO = 15.1%) of the Cu foil, the patterned Cu/Sn catalysts abruptly increased the FECO to 58.3% and suppressed the H2 evolution
(Table S2). Interestingly, when a 3-nm-thick Sn layer was deposited on the Cu foil without patterning, the FECO decreased to 2.9% and the FE of formate was as high as 91.6%. On the basis of these results, we believe that the exposure of both surfaces of Cu and Sn to the electrolyte is primarily required to achieve high FECO.
2.4. Geometrical Effect on the Electrochemical CO2 Reduction Reaction. To study the effect of geometric nanostructures on the catalytic properties, electrochemical activities of flat Cu−Sn, Cu−Sn rods, and 3D-h Cu−Sn catalysts with tc = 10 s were evaluated using linear-sweep voltammetry in the potential range of 0 to −1 VRHE in CO2purged 0.1 M KHCO3 solution (Figure 5a). The reductive
current density was higher on 3D-h Cu−Sn than on flat Cu− Sn and Cu−Sn rods over the entire potential range. In order to find the reason for the increased current density of 3D-h Cu− Sn catalysts, we measured the electrochemical surface area (ECSA) by the charge/discharge curves (Figure S14) and plotted the current densities at −0.3 VRHE as a function of the scan rate (Figure S15). Because the slope of the current density−scan rates curve indicates a double-layer capacitance that linearly correlates to ECSA, the porosity of electrocatalysts could be determined. The double-layer capacitance of 3D-h Cu−Sn (5.89 mF/cm2) was ∼15 times larger than that of the Cu−Sn rod (0.39 mF/cm2), meaning that the surface area of 3D-h is much larger than that of the Cu−Sn rod. FECO values of Cu foil, Cu rods, and 3D-h Cu were measured at potentials ranging from −0.15 to −1 VRHE. The highest FECO was 17.8% at −0.85 VRHE for the flat Cu, 5.2% at −0.7 VRHE for Cu rods, and 27.8% at −0.35 VRHE for 3D-h Cu (Figure S16a and Table S3). The highest FEH2 was 30.1% at −0.85 VRHE for the flat Cu, 33.9% at −0.7 VRHE for Cu rods, and 26.7% at −0.35 VRHE for 3D-h Cu (Figure S16b). Interestingly, the coating of Sn NPs (tc = 10 s) greatly increased the selectivity of CO and suppressed the HER on all
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsaem.0c00157 ACS Appl. Energy Mater. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
D
of the catalysts (Figures 5b and S17). The maximum FECO was 73.9% for flat Cu−Sn at −0.95 VRHE, 65% for the Cu−Sn rod at −0.9 VRHE, and 98.6% for 3D-h Cu−Sn at −0.45 VRHE (Table S4). On 3D-h Cu−Sn catalysts, CO is the dominant product over the entire potential range starting from −0.2 VRHE and extending to −1.0 VRHE. CO production on the 3D-h Cu−Sn catalyst sets in at remarkably low overpotentials that are ∼0.25 V less negative compared to the onset of the Cu−Sn rods. Also, 3D-h Cu−Sn catalysts achieved a significantly increased CO partial current density of −9.6 mA cm−2 and the outstanding production rate of CO (179.0 μmol h−1 cm−2) at −1.0 VRHE. This production rate is about 2.1 times higher than the maximum production rate of flat Cu−Sn (83.7 μmol h−1 cm−2) and Cu−Sn rods (83.6 μmol h−1 cm−2) (Figure S18). Moreover, the 3D-h Cu−Sn catalysts showed better stability than the Cu−Sn rods (Figure S19). The current density was almost constant and the FECO maintained a constant values of 96.0% at −0.45 VRHE even after 10 h of reaction. The morphology of 3D-h Cu−Sn changed slightly with prolonged reaction, but the 3D-h structure was maintained and the Sn NPs were still observed after the stability test (Figures S20 and S21). Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measure-
ments were performed to quantify the kinetics of electrontransfer processes. The Nyquist impedance plots were obtained in the frequency range from 200 kHz to 1 Hz with an amplitude of 30 mV (Figure 5c). The Nyquist plot in the highfrequency region represents the solution resistance (RS), and the semicircle in the low-frequency region represents the charge-transfer resistance (RCT) of the mass transfer during the electrocatalytic reaction. The 3D-h Cu−Sn had smaller impedance arcs in the second semicircle than di dthe flat Cu−Sn and the Cu−Sn rods, meaning that the 3D-h Cu−Sn has a lower RCT. To quantify the resistances, the EIS results were analyzed using an equivalent circuit model (Table S5).41,42 The RCT was 417.3 Ω cm2 for flat Cu−Sn, 87.2 Ω cm2 for Cu−Sn rods, and 60.6 Ω cm2 for 3D-h Cu−Sn; these results indicate that 3D-h Cu/Sn NP facilitates charge transfer in electrochemical CO2 RR. It was also discovered that the Tafel behavior of 3D-h Cu−Sn (205.3 mV/dec) showed a significantly smaller slope than that of flat Cu−Sn (259.3 mV/
dec), which means that 3D-h Cu−Sn requires less driving force (i.e., potential) to improve the reaction rate, indicating the intrinsically better activity (Figure 5d). In order to study the effect of 3D geometrical structure on
the local electric field and electrocatalytic reaction, we used a 3D finite-element-based solver with COMSOL Multiphysics. The surface of the structure was set to a constant potential of −0.3 V. Then, the electric field was calculated for the Cu rod (Figure 6a) and 3D-h Cu (Figure 6b). In the Cu rod, the electric field was intensified at the edge of the rods, but in 3D-h Cu, a strong electric field was localized at the tip of the branches. The total electric field (ETOT) was calculated by integrating over the surface of the structures (Figure 6c). The Cu rod had ETOT = 0.47 × 10
−5 V m, and 3D-h Cu had ETOT = 4.60 × 10−5 V m (i.e., ETOT was 9.8 times higher in 3D-h Cu than in the Cu rod). The localized electric field would activate the reaction by increasing the local concentration of K+ around the catalyst.11,43 To confirm the effect of the local electric field on the accumulation of K+ in the electrolyte, ICP-AES measurements were performed (Figure 6d). A potential of −1.0 VRHE was applied in a 0.1 M KHCO3 solution for 5 min, each sample was transferred to DI water with the applied potential, and then the potential was removed. The concentration of K+ was highest on the surface of the 3D-h Cu. These simulation and ICP-AES measurement results demonstrate that a strong localized electric field on the surface of 3D-h Cu induces K+ accumulation near the surfaces of catalysts. The adsorption of an inert cation such as K+ is known to raise the potential over the double layer with respect to the potential of the bulk electrolyte.44 This theory predicts that the increasing number of cations suppresses the hydrogen evolution by prohibiting the approach of the proton (H+) near the surface and promoting the CO2 reduction rate.
45 In particular, the local electric field induced by a cation near the electrode leads to a significant shift in the free energy of the *CO2 intermediate to a lower energy state such that the first step of CO2 reduction (CO2 → *CO2) is energetically favorable.46 Sequentially, these cations could shift the freeenergy landscape for the CO2 → CO reaction. 46−48
2.5. Discussion. Since CO and HCOOH are produced by parallel pathways on Cu−Sn catalysts, the selectivity of each
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsaem.0c00157 ACS Appl. Energy Mater. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
E
product is determined by key intermediates of *COOH and *OCHO, respectively. Recently, a density functional theory (DFT) calculation conducted by Qiao et al. showed that Sn donates electrons to Cu and is positively charged in the Cu− Sn alloys.49 The positively charged Sn sites hinder nucleophilic attack on the carbon and increase the thermodynamic barrier to *COOH adsorption. This DFT calculation can explain the results of 3D-h Cu−Sn catalysts: those with a high Cu/Sn ratio selectively produce CO, but those with a low Cu/Sn ratio prefer to produce HCOOH. Understanding the influence of the geometry on the catalytic properties is much more complicated due to various factors such as mass transport, local pH, and cationic effects.50 However, the presence of the local electric field and the increased cation (K+) concentration around 3D-h Cu−Sn can be one possible reason for enhanced CO production because it is reported that the local cationinduced field is energetically beneficial to the conversion of CO2 to CO.

sections.heading: 3. CONCLUSIONS
sections.text:
3D-h Cu−Sn catalysts have been fabricated to investigate the compositional and geometrical effects on the catalytic activity toward CO2 reduction. The CO selectivity of the bimetallic Cu−Sn system was discussed along with the surface coverage of Sn NPs on the Cu surface. The small Sn NPs, partially covering the Cu surface, significantly increased FECO from 24.1 to 98.6% at −0.45 VRHE. Thus, the low Cu/Sn ratio of the bimetallic Cu−Sn catalysts has been experimentally proven to be efficient for CO production. Furthermore, the hierarchical nanoscale geometry generates a strong localized electric field and causes K+ accumulation near the surfaces of catalysts. These cations could shift the free-energy landscape for the CO2 → CO reaction and facilitate the charge transfer between catalysts and the reactant. Although the enhanced CO selectivity cannot be fully understood due to various factors such as CO2 mass transport, the local pH, and uncoordinated crystal facets, the fact that the cation-induced electric field effect is highly relevant to the geometrical structure provides meaningful insights for future investigations. This study sheds light on the nature of bimetallic Cu−Sn for selective CO production and experimentally demonstrates the importance of composition and nanostructures that results in the enhanced electrochemical CO2 reduction performance.
